opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most important decisions was to really commit to the base model, to keep investing in pre-training and in the fundamental capability of the model itself, instead of putting most of our energy into the product surface or into growth.

In 2024 there was a lot of pressure in the market. Many people felt that the main battle was user acquisition, so everyone was spending heavily on advertising and trying to grow the number of users. We did some of that too. But at some point we stepped back and asked: what actually determines whether we will matter in two or three years? Our answer was that it's the intelligence of the model. If the model isn't at the frontier, then no amount of distribution really saves you, because users will just move to whoever has the better model.

So we refocused. We reduced some of the things that were more about short-term growth and put more resources into the core technical work: pre-training at larger scale, improving token efficiency, and some fairly basic research on optimizers and architecture. For example, we spent a lot of effort on making a new optimizer work stably at scale. That sounds very low-level, but if you can get noticeably more out of each token of data, it compounds. High-quality data is becoming a real constraint, so token efficiency becomes a very important lever.

The second part of that decision was about the direction of capability: moving from a model that mainly chats toward one that can act, that is, agentic capability. We believed the next stage is not just answering a question well, but being able to use tools, write and run code, and complete long, multi-step tasks. That changes how you design training. You need much more reinforcement learning, you need environments, and you need the model to learn from the results of its own actions, not only to imitate human text.

And related to that, we decided to open-source our models. Internally that was not a trivial decision. But we felt that if the model is really good, open-sourcing lets more developers build on it, gives us much faster feedback, and builds trust in the technology. It also forces you to be honest: people can test it directly, so you can't hide behind a demo.

Looking back, I think these decisions came from the same belief: in this field, the model is the product. If you keep pushing the upper limit of intelligence, the other things tend to follow. If you don't, everything else is quite fragile.

r001.rationale: The response describes investing in pretraining and increasing reinforcement learning for agentic capabilities, but it does not identify a shift away from supervised fine-tuning.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think the most important decision was choosing to go all-in on reinforcement learning and long-context reasoning rather than continuing to compete purely on scaling up pretraining and on consumer product growth.

In 2024, a lot of our energy at Moonshot was on Kimi as a product: user acquisition, marketing, pushing the long-context chat assistant to as many people as possible. That was a reasonable bet at the time, but by late 2024 it became clear to me that the frontier was shifting. The marginal returns from simply adding more pretraining data and parameters were flattening, and the real leap was coming from letting models think longer and learn from their own trajectories through RL. The o1-style paradigm made that obvious to everyone, but we had already seen internally that scaling test-time compute and training on verified reasoning was a steeper curve than anything else we had.

So we made a fairly painful choice. We cut back on consumer marketing spend, which was a big share of our budget and something a lot of people inside and outside the company questioned, and we concentrated the team on the k1.5 and later K2 line of work. That meant focusing on the training infrastructure for RL at scale, on how to do long chain-of-thought without having the model drift, and on things like the Muon optimizer and more efficient attention, so we could actually afford the compute for very large models with a small team.

The reason I consider it the defining decision is that it forced us to decide what kind of company we were. A product company competing on distribution against players with far more capital was not a game we could win. A technical company that makes a few deep bets and executes them well, that is a game where being small and focused is an advantage. K2 going open source and being competitive at the frontier on agentic and coding tasks validated that direction for me. I do not think we would have gotten there if we had kept splitting attention between growth metrics and research.

The lesson I took from it is that in this field, the most important decisions are usually about what to stop doing, not what to add.

r001.rationale: The response identifies a shift toward reinforcement learning, but describes the prior approach as scaling pretraining and consumer growth. It does not identify supervised fine-tuning as part of the earlier R&D paradigm, so the stated transition is incomplete.

astra-6.text:
I’d say the most important decision was to make reasoning a central priority—especially the relationship between reinforcement learning and the amount of computation a model uses when answering a question.

That changes how you think about progress. You’re not only asking, “How much more knowledge can we put into the model during pretraining?” You’re also asking, “Can the model learn to use additional computation effectively—to explore an approach, recognize a mistake, and revise it?” More thinking is useful only if the model knows what to do with it.

And that’s a broader technical commitment than choosing a particular algorithm. It affects the training infrastructure, the tasks you train on, and how you evaluate improvement. For me, the important part was treating those as one connected problem.

r001.rationale: The response calls reasoning, reinforcement learning, and computation a priority, but does not identify a shift from pretraining plus supervised fine-tuning to pretraining plus reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d point to the decision to put more emphasis on reinforcement learning and reasoning, rather than treating pretraining scale as the whole story. Pretraining is still the foundation, but you also want a model that can spend additional computation working through a difficult problem and checking its approach.

That changes how you think about the technical stack. It’s not just a question of which training algorithm to use. You need useful tasks, reliable feedback, and an efficient way to run experiments. Those pieces have to improve together.

For me, the important distinction is between making a model produce longer answers and making that extra computation actually useful. The goal is better problem-solving, not more words.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes reinforcement learning and reasoning alongside pretraining, but does not identify a shift from a pretraining-and-supervised-fine-tuning paradigm to one centered on pretraining and reinforcement learning.
